abstract: Insecticide resistance in malaria vectors is spreading, with newly identified resistance markers raising operational challenges and threatening malaria reduction. Anopheles arabiensis is an important vector in The Gambia; however, the molecular basis of its insecticide resistance remains poorly understood. We observed signals of population structure between coastal and inland An. arabiensis populations in The Gambia, indicating restricted gene flow likely influenced by environmental variation. Pyrethroid and DDT resistance were widespread. However, the prevalence of both phenotypic and genetic insecticide resistance differed between coastal and inland populations. For instance, the Vgsc-L995S and Vgsc-L995F substitutions conferring pyrethroid and DDT resistance were more frequent in coastal populations and were associated with markedly higher phenotypic resistance to these insecticides. We also identified increased frequencies of copy number variation at Cytochrome P450 (Cyp6aa/p, Cyp9k1) and carboxylesterase (Coeae2-7 g) metabolic resistance markers in coastal An. arabiensis. Some observed gene amplifications were unique to Gambian coastal populations, suggesting their independent evolution. Furthermore, we found evidence of genomic regions under recent positive selection on chromosomes 2L:37,282,152-37,298,202 and 3R:28,590,243-28,602,280 with more pronounced selection signals observed among coastal populations. Coastal populations of An. arabiensis displayed an enrichment of resistance alleles, suggesting a localised pressure driving the evolution, selection and spread of resistance mechanisms. These findings underscore the importance of genomic surveillance in concert with bioassays to inform targeted vector control interventions. They also highlight the need to identify the sources and impacts of insecticide pressure acting on recently detected genomic regions under selection in the coastal regions of The Gambia.
